title: First Unique Number
description: Design a data structure returning the first unique number in a growing stream, using a lazily-evicted queue of candidates.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a FirstUnique class, initialized with an array nums. Support showFirstUnique(), which returns the value of the first unique number in the stream seen so far (or -1 if none exists), and add(value), which appends a new number to the stream.

blocks.caption: A queue of candidate unique values is lazily cleaned of entries that have since become duplicates.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Constructor","nums[] (the initial stream)"],["add(value)","Appends value to the stream"],["showFirstUnique()","Returns the first value in stream order that has appeared exactly once so far, or -1"],["Goal","Both operations should run efficiently even with a long stream history"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

"First X so far in a growing stream" is a classic queue pattern: maintain candidates in arrival order, and lazily discard the front whenever it no longer satisfies the property being tracked (here, uniqueness). This mirrors the lazy-deletion idea used for priority structures, but with a plain FIFO queue instead of a heap, since order of first appearance (not priority) is what matters.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The exact same lazy-front-eviction pattern as Design Hit Counter, just evicting on "count exceeded 1" instead of "timestamp expired."
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a waiting line of values, each entering in the order first seen. If a value shows up again later, it loses its "unique" status, but rather than searching the line to remove it immediately, that cleanup is deferred until someone actually asks for the front of the line.

blocks.caption: A value that repeats loses its unique status, cleaned up only when queried.

items: A value enters the candidate queue only the FIRST time it is seen (its count goes from 0 to 1).
A count map tracks how many times each value has appeared in total.
showFirstUnique lazily pops the front of the queue while its count exceeds 1, since such entries are permanently disqualified once a value repeats.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Initial stream [2,3,5]. Then add(5), add(2), add(3), interleaved with showFirstUnique calls.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Queue after cleanup","Result"],"rows":[["showFirstUnique()","[2, 3, 5] (all unique)","2"],["add(5)","5 now has count 2, queue unchanged (5 already in queue, not re-added)","-"],["showFirstUnique()","[2, 3, 5], but 5 is stale","2 (front is still 2)"],["add(2)","2 now has count 2","-"],["showFirstUnique()","pop stale 2, pop stale 5, front is now 3","3"],["add(3)","3 now has count 2","-"],["showFirstUnique()","pop stale 3, queue now empty","-1"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The sequence of showFirstUnique results is [2, 2, 3, -1], matching the expected LeetCode example exactly.
5. How Should We Think?

A direct approach keeps the full history in order and, on every showFirstUnique call, scans it from the start looking for the first value with count exactly 1. This is correct but rescans potentially the entire history on every single query.

Since a value that becomes non-unique STAYS non-unique forever (counts only increase), a queue holding only values that were unique when first seen can be lazily cleaned: pop stale (now-duplicated) entries from the front until either the queue empties or a genuinely still-unique value is found. Each value is pushed once and popped at most once across the whole run, giving amortized O(1) per operation.
6. Brute Force Solution
Keep the full stream history in a list and a count map. On showFirstUnique, scan the history from the start for the first value with count exactly 1.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["add","O(1)","Appends to history and updates the count map"],["showFirstUnique","O(n)","n is the total stream length seen so far, rescanned every call"],["Space","O(n)","The full history list plus the count map"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: A long stream with many showFirstUnique calls repeats the same linear scan over already-checked-and-rejected duplicate entries every time.
8. Optimize the Solution

Maintain a queue containing only values that were unique at the moment they were first added. On add, push a new value only when its count transitions from 0 to 1. On showFirstUnique, pop stale entries (count > 1) from the front until the front is genuinely unique or the queue is empty, then return that front value or -1.

items: add(value): increment its count; push to the queue only if this is its first appearance (count becomes 1).
showFirstUnique(): pop stale front entries (count > 1), then return the front value, or -1 if the queue is empty.
Each value is pushed at most once and popped at most once across the entire run, giving amortized O(1) per operation.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: "First X so far" in a stream is a queue-of-candidates pattern with lazy eviction, whenever the disqualifying condition is one-directional (a value can lose eligibility but never regain it).
Only push a value to the candidate queue on its first appearance, avoiding duplicate queue entries entirely.
This same lazy-front-eviction idea (queue plus a source-of-truth count/state map) reapplies to any streaming "first valid item" query.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

First Unique Number is solved with a queue of candidate values (pushed only on first appearance) paired with a count map as the source of truth. showFirstUnique lazily discards front entries that have since become duplicates, giving amortized O(1) time per operation since each value is pushed and popped at most once across the whole stream.
